176.title: The grocer's parrot
176.hook: a parrot spills oil, is struck bald, and decides every bald man must have spilled oil too (Masnavi 1.247ff)
176.howItsDone: The grocer and the parrot is one of the Masnavi's short tales, and teachers use it to warn against judging others by oneself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hypocrisy: the pretending Marcus left behind, doing every act as if it were the last. Your line was as if the last.

You see someone crying in a parking lot and think: breakup, I've been there. A coworker is quiet in a meeting and you think: they're mad; I get quiet when I'm mad. It happens all day: assuming what's inside someone else is what would be inside you, usually without noticing. Rumi's second story in the Masnavi is short, funny, a little sharp, and about exactly this. It stars a bird. Today, the grocer's parrot.
screen: `CRYING IN A PARKING LOT.` → `THEY MUST FEEL WHAT I'D FEEL.` → `THE GROCER'S PARROT.`

segments.voice: A grocer had a parrot, green and clever, that chatted with the customers and kept an eye on the shop. One day, while the grocer was out, a cat dashed after a mouse. The parrot panicked, flapped across the counter, and knocked over the bottles of rose oil. Oil everywhere. The grocer came back, saw the mess, and in his anger struck the parrot on the head. Its head feathers fell out. It was bald, and it stopped talking. The grocer was heartbroken. He sighed, pulled at his beard, and gave money to the poor, hoping his parrot would speak again. Days went by in silence. Then a wandering dervish walked past the shop, his head completely shaved, bald and shining. And the parrot suddenly found its voice: hey, you! How did you end up bald? Did you spill oil from a bottle too? Everyone laughed. The parrot had made a comparison, a qiyas, and it was wrong. Same bald head, entirely different story. Here Rumi turns: don't measure the deeds of the holy by yourself. He adds a Persian pun. Sher and shir are written alike in the Persian script, yet one means lion and the other means milk. Two things can look the same on the page and be nothing alike. Rumi's worry is spiritual: people look at saints and prophets and say, they're just like us. But it works in a parking lot too. Before you decide what someone's going through, remember the parrot. Not the same bald.
screen: `A TALKING PARROT SPILLS THE OIL.` · `STRUCK BALD, IT FALLS SILENT.` · `DID YOU SPILL OIL TOO?` · `LION AND MILK, WRITTEN ALIKE.` · then, large: `NOT THE SAME BALD.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you've been judging lately, a relative, a neighbor, a person in the news, and notice the story you've told about why they are the way they are. Ask: is that their story, or mine? Imagine two or three other reasons for the same bald head and hold them loosely; you don't need the real one, just a looser grip on your first guess.
Qiyas, the Persian word for analogy, the false comparison the parrot made between two different bald heads. Today's word.
Your line: not the same bald. Lion and milk look alike on the page, too. Day one hundred seventy-six, done.

177.title: Only this moment
177.hook: Marcus: live three thousand years or three, you only lose the present you have (Meditations 2.14)
177.carry: am I here for the time I've got
177.howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations often return to 2.14 as a meditation on time, and it is widely quoted in modern Stoic practice alongside mindfulness teaching about attending to the present.

segments.voice: Yesterday, qiyas: the grocer's parrot, sure a bald dervish must have spilled oil too. Your line was not the same bald. Today closes the week.

A question people love to ask at dinner parties: if you could live a thousand years, would you? Some say yes, instantly. Think of the books, the places, the grandchildren's grandchildren. Others shudder. Underneath sits a fear many people carry quietly: that life is too short, that it's slipping away day by day, like sand. Marcus Aurelius took that fear seriously, and then did some very clear arithmetic with it. Today, only this moment.
screen: `WOULD YOU LIVE A THOUSAND YEARS?` → `LOSING LIFE LIKE SAND.` → `ONLY THIS MOMENT.`

segments.voice: Meditations 2.14 opens, in George Long's translation: "Though thou shouldst be going to live three thousand years, and as many times ten thousand years, still remember that no man loses any other life than this which he now lives, nor lives any other than this which he now loses." His reasoning: the past is already gone; you can't lose it, because you don't have it. The future isn't here yet; you can't lose that either. The only thing anyone ever has is the present moment, so it's the only thing anyone can lose. And the present, he says, is the same size for everyone. The emperor and the baby, the old woman and the young soldier, all have exactly now. That's why the longest life and the shortest, he concludes, come to the same thing when they end: each person gives up only the moment they're in. Comforting or unsettling? Probably both. But it changes the question. Not how much time will I get, but am I here for the time I've got. Now look back at this week. Rumi's king admitted the proud cures weren't working. His physician from the unseen found the truth by listening to a pulse as a name was spoken. Marcus reminded himself that his time has a limit, and to do each act as if it were the last. The grocer's parrot judged a stranger by its own old story instead of looking at him. A Muslim poet and a Roman emperor don't mean the same thing by any of it. But each, in his own way, kept asking for attention to what is actually here. Only this moment.
screen: `THREE THOUSAND YEARS OR THREE.` · `YOU ONLY HAVE THE PRESENT.` · `THE PRESENT IS THE SAME FOR ALL.` · `NOT HOW LONG, BUT AM I HERE.` · then, large: `ONLY THIS MOMENT.`

segments.voice: Feel your body where it sits, hear whatever sounds are here, notice the light. Let yesterday go for now, and let tomorrow wait; neither is here. Whenever your mind leaves, say inside, only this moment, and come back to this breath, this sound, this weight in the chair.
present moment, the one thing Marcus says anyone can ever have, or lose, however long they live. Today's word.
Your line: am I here for the time I've got. Next week, Rumi's lion, and a very small hare. A full week, done.

178.title: Trust, and tie your camel
178.hook: the animals tell the lion to trust God, and the lion answers that effort is also God's way (Masnavi 1.900ff)
178.howItsDone: The saying 'tie your camel, and trust in God' is recorded in al-Tirmidhi's hadith collection, and in the Masnavi the lion quotes it in a long debate about tawakkul, reliance on God, and effort.

segments.voice: Last week closed with Marcus's arithmetic: the present moment is all anyone ever loses. Your line was am I here for the time I've got.
screen: `AM I HERE FOR THE TIME I'VE GOT.`

segments.voice: Two people wait for the same job interview. One says whatever happens is meant to be, and doesn't prepare. The other rehearses for three nights, can't sleep, and is sure it all depends on them. Plenty of people swing between the two. Rumi's next story begins in a green valley, where the animals live in fear of a lion who hunts them whenever he likes. They go to him with an offer. And before the story can even start, the lion and the animals get into a long argument about exactly this. Today's word is tawakkul.
screen: `MEANT TO BE, OR ALL ON ME?` → `A LION IN A GREEN VALLEY.` → `TAWAKKUL.`

segments.voice: Tawakkul is an Arabic word for trust in God, relying on God, and in this story it starts an argument. The animals say to the lion: stop hunting us, and every day we'll send you one of us for your meal. The lion is suspicious. I've been cheated before, he says; I'll hunt, I'll do my part. The animals answer with tawakkul. Your effort is nothing, they say. Worry and scheming just show weak faith. Trust God, who feeds every creature. The lion answers back with a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. In the hadith collection of al-Tirmidhi, a man asks whether he should leave his camel untied and trust God, or tie it and trust God. The Prophet says: tie it, and trust. The lion builds on it. God gave us hands, he says; a ladder is set in front of us, and we're meant to climb it step by step. Effort isn't the opposite of trust; it's one of the ways trust is lived. The argument goes back and forth for many lines, and in the end the deal is struck. What Rumi leaves you with is both halves held together. The Quran says it in one line, in Pickthall's translation: "And when thou art resolved, then put thy trust in Allah." Decide, act, then let go of the part that isn't yours. Before the interview: prepare, then sleep. Tie your camel.
screen: `TAWAKKUL: TRUST IN GOD.` · `THE ANIMALS: JUST TRUST.` · `THE LION: TIE IT, AND TRUST.` · `EFFORT IS HOW TRUST IS LIVED.` · then, large: `TIE YOUR CAMEL.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're worried about and ask: what's my part? The call, the preparation, the conversation, the rope around the camel's knee; decide on it clearly. Then ask what isn't your part, other people's choices, the weather, the outcome, and if you pray, hand that part over to God; if you don't, just open your hands and let it rest.
Tawakkul. Trust in God, relying on God, which in Rumi's story and in the Prophet's saying goes hand in hand with effort. Today's word.
Your line: tie your camel. The rope and the trust go together. See you tomorrow.

179.title: The late hare
179.hook: the smallest animal walks to the lion slowly, on purpose (Masnavi 1)
179.howItsDone: The lion and the hare is a Masnavi story with older roots in the animal fables of Kalila and Dimna, which descend from the Indian Panchatantra; Rumi retells it with his own long reflections.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tawakkul: trust in God that goes hand in hand with effort. Tie your camel, then trust.

Have you ever been late on purpose? You let the pasta water boil a little longer so the argument in the kitchen could cool. You walked around the block before the meeting, so you'd walk in calm instead of furious. Something says hurry. But sometimes slowing down is exactly the right move. The animals have made their deal with the lion: one of them every day, chosen by lot. The days go by. Then the lot falls on a hare, small and easy to overlook. Today, the late hare.
screen: `LATE ON PURPOSE.` → `THE LOT FALLS ON THE HARE.` → `THE LATE HARE.`

segments.voice: The hare doesn't run and hide. He tells the other animals: give me a little time. I have a plan. They're outraged. Who do you think you are? We've kept our promise to the lion all this time, and you'll ruin it. You, a hare, cleverer than all of us? The hare answers calmly: God gives understanding to the weak as well as the strong. Rumi, through him, points to the bee: a tiny creature, and yet, the Quran says, God inspired it to build and make honey. Size isn't wisdom. So they let him go. And he walks. Slowly. He stops. He thinks. He lingers. Meanwhile the lion waits, hour after hour, no meal. He paces, roars, claws the ground. I knew it, he says to himself. They cheated me. I'll never trust them again. Rumi spends lines on that rage: how anger blinds, and how being sure of yourself can make you easy to fool. By the time the hare finally strolls up, the lion is almost out of his mind. Why are you late? he roars. The hare bows and begins a story, which comes tomorrow. For today, notice the strategy. The hare can't outfight the lion, and he can't outrun him forever. But he can choose his pace, and the lion can't. He slows down on purpose, and the lion's own hurry becomes his weakness.
screen: `GIVE ME TIME: I HAVE A PLAN.` · `THE BEE: SMALL, AND INSPIRED.` · `THE HARE WALKS SLOWLY.` · `THE LION'S RAGE BLINDS HIM.` · then, large: `THE LATE HARE.`

segments.voice: Take the next thing you do, standing up, reaching for your phone, even the next breath, and do it at half speed. Notice the urge to hurry; let it be there, and don't obey it. Breathe out slower than you'd like, and feel what it's like to set your own pace.
Masnavi, Rumi's book of stories: the hare chosen for the lion walks to him slowly, on purpose, while the lion's rage grows. Today's word.
Your line: he slows down on purpose. Small, slow, and with a plan. Day one hundred seventy-nine, done.

screen: `DAY 179 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LION IN THE WELL.`

180.title: The lion in the well
180.hook: the hare shows the lion his own reflection in a well, and he leaps at it (Masnavi 1)
180.howItsDone: Teachers of the Masnavi often use the lion at the well to teach that the faults we see in others can reflect our own, pairing it with the saying that the believer is a mirror to the believer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Masnavi's late hare walked slowly to the lion, and the lion's own hurry became his weakness.

Somewhere at work there's a person who drives you up the wall. Always interrupting. Always needing to be right. Always making it about themselves. And late one night, a small, unwelcome thought slips in: do I do that? It's tempting to slam the door on that thought. Rumi doesn't. The hare has arrived, very late, before a lion half mad with hunger. Why are you late? the lion roars. And the little hare, bowing, begins his story. Today, the lion in the well.
screen: `THE ONE WHO DRIVES YOU UP THE WALL.` → `DO I DO THAT?` → `THE LION IN THE WELL.`

segments.voice: Your majesty, I set out on time, with another hare as your meal. But on the road another lion stopped us. I told him we belong to the king of beasts. He laughed: who's your king? I'm the king here. He took my friend, and I barely got away to tell you. The lion is beside himself. Another lion, in my valley? Show me. So the hare leads him to a deep well. At the edge he hangs back and trembles. He's in there, the hare whispers, with my friend. The lion, in some tellings, tucks the hare under his arm for courage, and looks down. In the dark water a lion glares up at him, with a hare in its grip. He lets go of the real hare, roars, and leaps at the enemy. The water closes over him. The little hare runs home to the valley, and the animals rejoice. Then Rumi turns to us. The lion attacked his own face: he took his reflection for a rival and destroyed himself fighting it. So many of the faults you see in others, Rumi says, are your own nature looking back at you. You leap at the reflection and drown in your own anger. He points to a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: the believer is a mirror to the believer. What bothers you in someone else may be showing you yourself. That doesn't mean every fault you see is yours; sometimes the coworker really is rude. But before you leap, it's worth leaning over the well and asking: is that my face?
screen: `ANOTHER LION TOOK MY FRIEND.` · `THE HARE LEADS HIM TO A WELL.` · `HE LEAPS AT HIS OWN FACE.` · `WHAT YOU SEE MAY BE YOU.` · then, large: `THAT'S MY FACE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who really bothers you, and name the exact thing: controlling, careless, loud, always late. Then gently lean over the well: is there a place in your life where you do some version of that too? You don't have to find one; if you do, don't scold yourself, just say inside, that's my face, and notice what happens to the anger.
Mirror. A saying of the Prophet Muhammad: the believer is a mirror to the believer, showing back what's really our own. Today's word.
Your line: that's my face. Sometimes the well is a mirror. That's day one hundred eighty.

181.title: The lion inside
181.hook: Rumi ends: the outer enemy is gone, the lion within remains, the greater struggle (Masnavi 1.1373ff)
181.carry: a dragon that could drink the seas
181.howItsDone: In Sufi teaching, the struggle with the nafs, the grasping self, is described as the greater jihad, and the end of Rumi's lion and hare story is read by Sufi teachers as a statement of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mirror: the lion leaped at his own reflection and drowned. What bothers you in someone else may be your own face.

You finally deal with the thing. You quit the job with the awful boss. You move out from the terrible roommate. You block the person who kept upsetting you. For a week, it's wonderful. Then you notice the anger is still there. The worry is still there. The old habit is right where you left it. The problem packed its bags and came along. The animals are dancing in the valley. The lion is gone. And Rumi, instead of ending the story, turns and speaks straight to his listeners. Today, the lion inside.
screen: `YOU FINALLY DEAL WITH THE THING.` → `IT PACKED ITS BAGS AND CAME ALONG.` → `THE LION INSIDE.`

segments.voice: In plain words, Rumi says: we've killed the enemy outside, but inside there's an enemy worse than him. The clever hare can't trick this one into a well; wit and reason alone won't defeat it. Rumi's word for it is nafs. In Arabic and Persian it means the self or the soul, and in Sufi teaching it often means the grasping, demanding part of the self: the appetite that's never full, the pride that has to win, the anger that roars first. Rumi calls it a dragon that could drink the seas and still burn. Then he cites a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, spoken on coming home from a battle: we have returned from the lesser struggle to the greater struggle. The word there is jihad, which means striving or struggle, and the greater one, in this saying, is the struggle with your own self. A note on the source: the saying is loved among Sufis, but hadith scholars have judged its chain of transmission weak, and it isn't in the major collections. Rumi uses it. Some treasure its meaning; others question its source. Now put the story together: a lion, a clever hare, a well, a reflection. The outer lion was never really the danger. The one to watch is the one you carry everywhere, the one who would have leaped at the reflection too. That, for Rumi, is the greater struggle. The lion inside.
screen: `AN ENEMY WORSE, WITHIN.` · `NAFS: THE GRASPING SELF.` · `THE LESSER AND GREATER STRUGGLE.` · `A LOVED SAYING, A WEAK CHAIN.` · then, large: `THE LION INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Ask quietly: what in me roars first? Anger, maybe, or wanting more, or needing to be right, or fear dressed up as control. Don't fight it now; just see it and name it, the way you would name an animal you're going to learn to live with, then breathe low into your belly and notice what changes when you're still.
Nafs. The grasping, demanding self that Sufi teaching says is harder to defeat than any outer enemy. Today's word.
Your line: a dragon that could drink the seas. The greater struggle is the one inside. See you tomorrow.

182.title: The cracked loaf
182.hook: Marcus: even the cracks in baked bread and the split of a ripe fig have their own beauty (Meditations 3.2)
182.howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations often cite 3.2 as Marcus's reflection on beauty in the unplanned and the aging, and modern Stoic practice uses it to train a kinder way of seeing ordinary imperfection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nafs: the outer lion drowned, and Rumi pointed at the grasping self each of us carries, a dragon that could drink the seas.

Picture a loaf of bread just out of the oven. Not the perfect factory kind. The real kind, where the crust has burst open along the top in a rough, golden split. Is that the ugly part, or the part you want to tear off first? Nobody planned that crack. The baker was aiming for a smooth loaf. But the split is where it looks most alive. An emperor at war, in a tent on the frontier, stopped to write about exactly this. Today, the cracked loaf.
screen: `A LOAF JUST OUT OF THE OVEN.` → `THE CRUST BURST OPEN.` → `THE CRACKED LOAF.`

segments.voice: Book three of the Meditations opens with a surprising little essay on beauty. Even the side effects of nature, Marcus says, the things nobody intended, have a charm of their own. His first example, in George Long's translation: "when bread is baked some parts are split at the surface." Those cracks run against the baker's art. And yet they're beautiful in their own way, and somehow they make you hungry. Then he keeps going, like someone who can't stop noticing. Ripe figs that split open. Olives near the point of spoiling, which is exactly when they're richest. Ears of wheat bending down. The wrinkled brow of a lion. The foam at a wild boar's mouth. And the particular ripeness and grace of old men and old women, which a person with the right eyes can see. Why does a Stoic emperor care about split bread? For the Stoics, everything that happens comes from one nature, one order running through the world. Understand that, and you stop dividing things into the planned and the spoiled, the smooth and the broken. You see the whole. The crack belongs to the loaf. The wrinkle belongs to the face. The worn edge belongs to the life. That goes for your own body in the mirror, your parents getting older, the thing you made that didn't come out as planned. The cracked loaf.

segments.voice: Look around and find something worn, chipped, faded or cracked: a mug with a chip, a scuffed shoe, your own hands. Look at it the way Marcus looked at the bread, not for what's wrong with it but for what's alive in it, and what story the crack tells. Stay with it until you see something you'd have missed.
Ripeness. Marcus noticed it even in old age, in cracked bread and split figs: the beauty of things worn by time. Today's word.
Your line: ripe figs that split open. What nobody planned can still be beautiful. Day one hundred eighty-two, done.
